BREAKING: This past week's -10.4% drop in the Nasdaq 100 was one of the rarest weekly declines in 40 years.

Of the last 2,133 trading weeks, just 11 saw declines of this magnitude or worse.

That's 0.52% of all weeks, a 3.27 standard deviation move based on the historical mean and volatility.

Of course, market returns exhibit "fat tails," meaning extreme moves occur more frequently than a normal distribution would predict.

However, even accounting for the fact that extreme market moves are more common than traditional statistical models suggest, this was a historically rare selloff.

Volatility returns when markets least expect it.

Investor positioning in copper is cratering:

Speculative investors sold -$1.3 billion in Comex copper futures in the week ending November 10th, marking the 7th consecutive weekly sale.

This group includes hedge funds, commodity trading advisers (CTAs), and other institutional investors.

Since September 22nd, they have sold a cumulative -$10.8 billion.

This brings long speculative investor positioning down to ~$5.2 billion, its lowest since October 2025.

Meanwhile, copper futures fell -5.3% on Wednesday, marking their largest daily decline since July 2026.

Copper prices are now down -18.2% from their September peak, to $5.67 per pound, their lowest level since April.

The copper market is seeing a massive shift in sentiment.

The semiconductor trade is still popular among fund managers:

39% of global fund managers said "long global semiconductors" was the most crowded trade, according to a BofA survey of 169 fund managers overseeing $461 billion in assets conducted between November 6th and November 12th.

This marks the 6th consecutive month that semiconductors have held the top spot.

However, this figure is down from the 82% peak recorded in July this year.

Meanwhile, “Short China Stocks” ranked 2nd for the first time, with 14% of respondents identifying it as the most crowded trade.

By comparison, "Long Magnificent 7" and "Short Treasuries" were considered the most crowded trades just by 12% and 10% of fund managers, respectively.

Investor appetite for semiconductor stocks remains strong.

BREAKING: The 3-month correlation between the S&P 500 and gold is up to +0.35, doubling since February.

The correlation between these two assets has remained positive throughout the year, unlike in 2025, when it was negative for most months.

Since the Iran War began, gold has increasingly traded like a risky asset rather than a hedge against market declines, moving alongside equities.

Year-to-date, gold prices are now down -17%, on track for their biggest annual decline since 2013.

This comes as elevated energy prices, resurging inflation, and rising interest rates have heavily weighed on gold.

Furthermore, recent equity market losses have forced some investors to liquidate gold holdings to offset losses elsewhere.

Gold is caught up in the liquidity crunch.

BREAKING: The US Department of Agriculture was hit by a cyberattack this week, raising concerns that hackers accessed "sensitive information" at the agency, per NBC News.

The USDA informed employees on Thursday that a system the agency uses to facilitate payments to farmers was breached.

They warned that accessing the payments system could provide hackers with a backdoor to reaching more sensitive material.

It is not yet known who is responsible for the hack.

BREAKING: Nvidia, $NVDA, sets a new record for the largest-ever loss of market cap in a stock in 45 days.

The stock has now lost -$2.8 trillion in market cap from its high seen on October 6th.

There have been 33 trading days since October 6th, meaning Nvidia has lost an average of -$85 billion per day, for 33 trading days in a row.

Furthermore, Nvidia has accounted for ~40% of the S&P 500's market cap losses since its record high on October 6th.

That's one way to make history.

What's rather unique about the market correction over the last 45 days is that the market is no longer waiting on President Trump to intervene.

In every major market downturn since January 2025, President Trump has had the ability to intervene and mark a bottom. And, that's almost always what happened.

This includes the trade war, Iran War, Greenland situation, US-China tensions, interest rates, Venezuela, and more.

In our X Article earlier today, we named this financial backstop the "Trump Put."

Minutes ago, President Trump held a press conference and mentioned Iran, Nvidia, China, and Ukraine, but never markets.

With the shift in political power in the US, the era of the "Trump Put" appears to be nearing its end.

The erosion of this backstop for financial markets partially explains why selling pressure has been so strong this week.

This will be a major adjustment for investors.

Last several posts featured weekly scale charts and breakouts. Breakout confirmations are decided intr-week on a daily close above the threshold.

"Last full day low" is the low of the full day before the breakout confirmation day.

It is not a magical number. It serves as some wiggle room in case there is volatility right after the breakout. It can be utilized as a protective stop.

At the time of the breakout, it is hard to know if the breakout will fail or succeed. It is usually following the breakout, the follow through with momentum that offers more insight into the type of trend we are dealing with. 

As I mentioned in previous posts, utilizing last full day low as a protective stop is what you can control.
